column3: It is the near-verbatim parallel: denial of the truth is followed by the arrival of the news they mocked.
It makes the mocked matter become an enclosing consequence, clarifying how the announced news comes upon its mockers.
It shows mockery as a recurring response to every arriving prophet, supplying the repeated rejection pattern behind the focus.
It adds that the evil of their own deeds befalls them as the mocked matter closes around them.
Musa's account of his past act does not clarify the rejection or arriving consequence in the focus.
It independently states the habitual mockery of every messenger, though that pattern is already established above.
It links an evil outcome to denying and mocking Allah's signs, extending the focus's causal sequence.
The command to approach Pharaoh belongs to the later Musa narrative, not the focus's stated consequence.
Its charge of fabricating a lie concerns unsupported worship claims rather than mocking an announced consequence.
Its lament over recurring mockery of messengers adds the accumulated loss produced by the pattern.
It shows a defensive social use of mockery against a messenger, but not the subsequent arrival of the mocked news.
Yusuf's advance report of food does not illuminate denial or ridicule in the focus.
It shows liars exposed against themselves, a limited consequence parallel without the focus's announced news.
As the immediately preceding ayah, it supplies their turning away from each renewed reminder before the focus calls that response denial.
It contrasts presumptuous denial of the Hour with later reporting and severe punishment, but is not a direct ridicule parallel.
It directly joins delayed punishment, mockery of that delay, and the day it arrives and surrounds them.
Pharaoh's reminder of Musa's upbringing does not develop the focus's denial or mockery.
It supplies a later reporting of forgotten deeds, but not the mocked announcement or its arrival.
It situates denial among earlier messengers and their eventual divine help, without the focus's mockery-to-consequence turn.
The failed call to partners and sight of punishment offers a judgment-scene parallel only.
It states the repeated turning away from arriving signs, the antecedent response that 26:5-6 sharpens.
It shows prior denial preventing later belief despite clear messengers, explaining the persistence of the focus's response.
Pharaoh's accusation against Musa does not clarify the focus's collective denial and awaited consequence.
Divine sufficiency against mockers concerns protection of the messenger rather than the consequence that reaches mockers.
It notes that rejection by one group does not exhaust the reception of revelation, but adds little to the focus.
Musa's fear of being called a liar supplies a later narrative echo of the falsification named in the focus.
The challenge to produce alleged partners is not materially connected to the focus's news and mockery.
It defends the messenger's delivery of recitation, without the focus's denial-to-consequence movement.
The question about answering messengers adds accountability, but not the particular mocked report.
It concerns associating with those who treat religion as mockery, not their later reckoning.
The ruling on association does not clarify the focus's denial or arriving news.
The clear Book is the disclosed message that the following ayat say is turned away from and denied.
It gives a general penalty for treating signs and messengers as mockery, already covered more directly by earlier cards.
The repeated ruling on association does not develop the focus's sequence.
The request concerning the Children of Israel belongs to the later Musa commission.
Its family-pressure and final-account setting does not clarify the focus's mocked announcement.
It repeats the enclosing return of what they mocked, but adds little after 45:33 and 16:34.
It supplies a distinct case of knowingly speaking falsehood about revelation, only loosely related to denial.
The introduction to Musa's story does not add to the focus's denial and consequence.
It directly states that what was mocked surrounded the mockers, though it is redundant with earlier fuller parallels.
Naming Pharaoh's people does not add to the focus's general statement.
It connects treating a sign as mockery with humiliating punishment, specifying the retributive form.
It repeats the same surrounding consequence for mocking messengers, already supplied more fully above.
Musa's commission to the wrongdoing people belongs to the later narrative rather than the focus's claim.
The recited report of Nuh offers a precedent for warning hearers, but does not itself explain mockery's consequence.
It shows confident reception of one's own knowledge giving way to the very thing mocked, a close alternate setting.
The Prophet's grief over their unbelief does not clarify the stated arrival of the mocked news.
The failure of invoked partners and a reliable informer is not a close link to the focus.
It repeats denial of the truth when it arrives, supplying the immediate cognitive state before its later fulfillment.
The earth's diverse growth follows the focus as a sign but does not explain its denial-and-news statement.
Its great news gives a broad conceptual parallel, but lacks the focus's denial and mockery sequence.
It gives a compact precedent of denial followed by destructive consequence.
The condemned group's confession of error does not identify the denied or mocked announcement.
It distinguishes a serious divine command from an accusation of mockery, a limited reversal of the focus's posture.
It joins denial of signs to punishment, but does not add the mocked report's eventual arrival.
It provides the immediate alternative of an overwhelming sign that would force submission, framing the voluntary refusal in the focus.
It states that people defer belief until the precedent of earlier punishment or punishment itself comes before them.
Its terse disbelief followed by future knowledge is a general, already-covered consequence pattern.
The closing description of the Lord does not clarify the focus's denial or arriving news.
Adam's taught names and the demand for information do not add to the focus.
It gives another narrative instance where denial is followed by a decisive destructive event.
The destruction of stronger predecessors supports the warning horizon, but is less specific than earlier cards.
The prohibition on abusing rules of divorce does not illuminate the focus's ridicule and consequence.
It repeats the enclosing return of what was mocked, but its added theme of unusable faculties is peripheral here.
Musa's concern about speech and Harun belongs to the subsequent commission narrative.
It offers a reciprocal consequence for neglecting received signs, without the focus's mocking response.
Its later statement that they would not believe even if it were recited to them confirms the persistence of refusal in this surah.
The reassurance and command to go with signs do not clarify the focus's declared consequence.
The promise of guidance and safety to followers is not a close connection after the earlier cards.
It invokes the historical outcome of peoples who denied messengers, preserving the warning of realized rejection.
It identifies treating Allah's signs as mockery as the reason for an inescapable present punishment.
It frames the questioned matter as certain and inescapable, clarifying the force of the future arrival in the focus.
It says denial precedes both comprehension and fulfillment, directly explaining why the mocked matter has not yet come.
Musa's fear of being killed is part of his later personal response to the commission.
The disclosure of Adam's knowledge does not bear on denial or ridicule of an announced matter.
It repeats that prior denial blocks reception of later clear messengers, adding little beyond 7:101.
The woe for a habitual lying sinner is only contextual to the nearby mockery passage.
The command to report Abraham's guests does not clarify the focus's consequence.
It ties denial of signs and the meeting of the Hereafter to the nullification and recompense of deeds.
Calling the revealed message ancient tales gives a concrete dismissive response parallel to the focus's denial.
Divine sufficiency for the Prophet and believers does not develop the focus's message.
It supplies a warning-neglect and punishment precedent, but not the focus's denied news.
The loss of reports in the final scene contrasts with the report that comes in the focus, without a direct explanatory link.
The command to recite Abraham's story starts another narrative and adds no direct clarification.
It joins mockery to an awaited disclosure of what mockers fear, a close disclosure-and-exposure parallel.
The assertion of Allah's complete knowledge does not clarify denial of the announced news.
Musa's receiving the Book does not add to the focus after its immediate context is already represented.
It presents accumulated reports of earlier peoples, clear messengers, and self-incurred ruin as warning precedent.
The statement of peace over life's stages does not develop the focus's rejection or consequence.
Its instruction to pardon until Allah's command arrives is not a close link to the focus.
The messenger's recitation and teaching of signs provides the positive counterpart to their rejection, but adds little here.
The judgment of excuses and deeds is a different reporting context from the mocked announced matter.
The marital exception does not relate to the focus.
It warns of sudden, enveloping punishment, but not its connection to mocked revelation.
The statement about futile worship does not clarify the focus's denial and arriving news.
The destructive wind image lacks a denial, mockery, or announced-report connection.
The dispute over the sleepers' number does not add to the focus.
It ends with reporting deeds at return, but its primary concern is reciprocal insult rather than the focus's mockery.
The inquiry into Yusuf's case does not clarify the focus.
The future disclosure to Yusuf's brothers offers a distant reversal through later news, but not the focus's denial pattern.
It directly pairs mockery of earlier messengers with a period of respite and then divine seizure, closely explaining the focus's future arrival.
It explicitly answers present ridicule with the certainty that the ridiculers will later know whom punishment reaches.
It completes the previous challenge by naming the humiliating punishment and enduring chastisement that will come upon them.
The demand to know when the promise will occur gives a concrete form of treating the announced consequence as dismissible delay.
It answers that demand with the sudden arrival that will confound the deniers and cannot be repelled.
It names taking Allah's signs and messengers as mockery as the disbelievers' mode of resistance.
It records the direct social act of taking the messenger as an object of mockery.
It shows an organized attempt to prevent the Qur'an from being heard so that rejection can prevail.
It gives the punishment of those who denied Allah's signs, supplying the retributive horizon of the focus.
It turns the recurring mockery of prophets into a stated divine retribution against earlier deniers.
The people of Nuh deny their messenger and are followed by a decisive destructive precedent.
The denial of Hud by 'Ad and their punishment supplies another compressed historical realization of the focus's warning.
Thamud's denial of warnings and its stated consequence preserve the warning-to-realization pattern.
The people of Lut deny warnings and meet punishment, extending the repeated precedent of denied announcement.
It immediately illustrates that denial is not merely verbal: earlier generations were destroyed and replaced.
It states that prior generations were destroyed after their messengers brought clear proofs and they still would not believe.
It exposes the incoherence of believing only after the hastened punishment has actually occurred.
It gives the skeptical challenge, "When is this promise?", that turns a future warning into an object of dismissal.
It answers with the sudden blast that seizes them while they are still disputing, a close realization parallel.
It states that earlier peoples denied and punishment came upon them from where they did not perceive.
It shows belief attempted only once punishment is seen, too late to undo the preceding denial.
It depicts the promised matter brought near to the disbelievers, whose faces are distressed as they are told this is what they called for.
The people of Nuh are introduced as deniers of the messengers, beginning the repeated historical pattern developed through the rest of this surah.
